A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same MemNO research. Their complete main texts and appendices are readable, allowing methods, proofs, experiments and displays to be matched despite substantial reorganization.

before.justification: V1 reports original KS, Burgers and Navier-Stokes experiments, including resolution and noise studies and appendix architecture ablations.

after.justification: V2 reports original predictive experiments, additional architecture and memory ablations, computational measurements and Fourier-spectrum analyses.

M1.justification: The central MemNO framework and S4FFNO design are retained. V2 adds an S4U-Net instantiation and experimental variants using input gradients, a convolutional encoder or a convolution before memory (Appendices G.3 and H). These are limited architectural extensions rather than a replacement of the method.

E1.justification: The original KS, Burgers and Navier-Stokes studies remain. Appendix D substantially expands the datasets analyzed through PDEBench Advection and Reaction-Diffusion, additional Burgers viscosities, and PDE-Refiner KS datasets at viscosities 0.5 and 1.0. This expansion primarily concerns spectral analysis, rather than fully documented predictive benchmarks.

E2.justification: V2 Table 1 adds evaluated Factformer, Galerkin Transformer, U-Net and four-input FFNO comparisons to the original FFNO/S4FFNO comparison for KS and Burgers. The LSTM and Transformer memory alternatives are retained from v1's appendix, not newly introduced comparisons.

E3.justification: The main KS experiment's reported horizon changes from 5 to 2.5 seconds, with temporal spacing changing from 0.2 to 0.1. V2 introduces four-observation initialization for Multi Input FFNO, memory-window controls and FFNO width/depth sweeps. The Fourier cutoff used in the diagnostic ω_f also changes. These establish substantial reported protocol changes without establishing that every retained experiment was rerun.

E4.justification: V2 adds memory-window and model-capacity controls (Sections 6.1.1–6.1.2), spectral profiling of common datasets (Appendix D), an S4U-Net ablation (G.3), and tests of explicit spatial-information mechanisms (H). These investigate substantially more explanations for memory's benefits. The original sequential-model and memory-placement ablations remain.

E5.justification: V1 Figure 1 explicitly reports three-seed averages and standard-deviation shading; corresponding v2 Figure 2 omits both that disclosure and the bands. Burgers uncertainty bands also disappear. The memory-placement table retains its three-seed mean and standard-deviation reporting. This establishes reduced reporting, not necessarily fewer experimental runs.

E6.justification: Main KS and Burgers results are replaced, and numerous comparator, ablation, timing and spectral results are added. For KS viscosity 0.1 at resolution 32, Table 1 changes FFNO/S4FFNO errors from 0.376/0.079 to 0.446/0.108, but the reported horizon differs, preventing a same-setting comparison. V1 Table 2's placement-ablation results remain unchanged in v2 Table 4.

T1.justification: The principal theorem, propositions and proof are retained after relocation. V2 adds an algorithmic-complexity derivation in Appendix B.2. Equation 14 also revises ω_f's included frequencies from |n| >= f/2 to |n| > floor(f/2), while expressing temporal averaging separately.

C1.justification: The central claim that memory benefits partially observed, high-frequency PDE dynamics remains. V2 adds challenging-benchmark construction as an explicit headline contribution and broadens its performance claims to comparisons with other memory models and larger memoryless models.

C2.justification: V2 adds interpretations attributing gains to accessible history rather than parameter capacity, discusses benchmark warm-up and initial spectra, and interprets unsuccessful spatial-information variants. It explicitly qualifies ω_f as a useful heuristic that cannot alone determine memory importance. These substantially expand the explanations and applicability boundaries beyond v1.

D1.justification: V2 adds detailed comparator implementations, MemNO pseudocode, a forked data-generator link and explicit KS generation command. It also documents the L40S timing-benchmark setup, additional architecture hyperparameters and fuller GPU-memory explanations. These substantially improve implementation documentation, although some setting descriptions remain inconsistent.

R1.justification: V2 substantially expands positioning against classical and learned Mori-Zwanzig closure methods, including Gouasmi, Parish and Duraisamy, Beck, Pan and Duraisamy, and Gupta and Lermusiaux. It distinguishes its approach from hybrid and adjoint-based closures and connects its benchmark contribution to McGreivy and Hakim's critique of PDE evaluation.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction and experimental narrative are extensively rewritten. Theory moves before the method, while dataset construction, training and architecture are regrouped under Experimental Setup. The framework and S4FFNO instantiation receive separate subsections, and periodic boundary conditions move to an appendix.

P2.justification: V2 adds an architecture diagram, memory-window plot, dataset-spectrum heatmap and pseudocode display. Table 1 is substantially redesigned to combine KS and Burgers with additional comparators and memory indicators; new capacity, timing and architecture tables accompany expanded comparison plots. These exceed simple renumbering or numerical updates.

improvement.justification: Broader baselines and the new memory-length, capacity and U-Net controls substantially strengthen attribution of the gains to memory, addressing an important weakness in v1's evidence. Spectral profiling and implementation guidance further improve usefulness. These gains outweigh reduced uncertainty reporting and isolated inconsistencies, such as FFNO's resolution-64 error differing between v2 Tables 1 and 6. The changed KS horizon prevents interpreting revised scores as same-setting performance gains.
